name: LISQM
full_name: List of Implementations of Sound Quality Metrics
tagline: A List of Open-Source Implementations of Psychoacoustic and Sound Quality Metrics
description: A list of open-source implementations of psychoacoustic metrics, also called sound quality (SQ) metrics: loudness, sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength, tonality, impulsiveness and psychoacoustic annoyance. Each implementation is listed under the standard edition or model it follows. All programming languages.
credit: Developed by Zhenxian LI with assistance from Claude Code.
ordering: Implementations and projects are listed by group: established, newly released, developing, legacy, others, status unknown. Newly released projects were first released less than about a year ago and are not yet seen to be widely used in the community. Legacy projects are archived or have had no commit for three years or more; the projects with a highlight (shown in bold on the website) and reference programs are never legacy. Within each group the projects with a highlight come first, then ranked and active ones. Projects in the others group do not compute the metrics themselves; they call another listed project (listed in calls), and their rows appear under also_through instead of implementations. Projects in the unknown group could not be opened (access); they list a claim and no implementations.

standing.established: Described in a publication, used by others, or written by the authors of the model, with more than a year of history.
standing.newly-released: First released less than about a year ago, and not yet seen to be widely used in the community.
standing.developing: Public for more than a year, but without a publication or documented use by others: research, teaching or personal code.

group.established: Described in a publication, used by others, or written by the authors of the model, with more than a year of history.
group.newly-released: First released less than about a year ago, and not yet seen to be widely used in the community.
group.developing: Public for more than a year, but without a publication or documented use by others: research, teaching or personal code.
group.legacy: Archived, or no commit for three years or more. Kept for reference: the code may follow an older edition and may not run with current software.
group.others: Tools that do not compute the metrics themselves: interfaces, front ends and wrappers that call one of the listed projects.
group.unknown: Projects whose code could not be opened, for example because the repository needs a login. What they implement is unverified, so they are listed with what they claim and not under the metrics.

kind.library: Functions to call from your own code: a Python package, a MATLAB toolbox, or a C, C++, C#, Rust or Julia library.
kind.research-code: Code published with a study, a thesis or a student project, to run or adapt; not packaged as a library.
kind.application: A program to run, with a graphical or command-line interface; no programming needed.
kind.plugin: Runs inside other software: a plug-in for an audio workstation, or a Pure Data external.
kind.reference-program: Code published with a standard or by the authors of the model, as the reference for it.

status.available: In the latest release, or on the default branch of a project without releases.
status.unreleased: Merged on the default branch but newer than the latest release.
status.proposed: Open pull request or separate branch, not merged.

validation.standard-data: Compared with test signals or values published in the standard or the model paper.
validation.reference-code: Compared with the reference program or the model authors' own code.
validation.cross-implementation: Compared with another implementation, named where the project says which. Agreement shows that both compute the same values, not that either follows the standard.
validation.self-tests: Tests exist, but without external reference data.
validation.not-stated: The project does not say how it was validated.

access.restricted: The repository cannot be opened without a login.

families.name: Loudness
families.summary: How loud a sound is perceived, in sone (loudness) and phon (loudness level). Four model families are standardised: Zwicker (ISO 532-1), Moore–Glasberg (ISO 532-2), Moore–Glasberg–Schlittenlacher (ISO 532-3) and the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2).

families.name: Sharpness
families.summary: The sensation produced by high-frequency content, in acum. Standardised in DIN 45692 on top of Zwicker loudness; ECMA-418-2 does not define sharpness.

families.name: Roughness
families.summary: The sensation produced by fast amplitude or frequency modulation (roughly 15 to 300 Hz, strongest near 70 Hz), in asper.

families.name: Fluctuation strength
families.summary: The sensation produced by slow modulation (below about 20 Hz, strongest near 4 Hz), in vacil.

families.name: Tonality
families.summary: How prominent tonal components are. Covers psychoacoustic tonality models (Aures, ECMA-418-2) and the engineering measures used for product noise (tone-to-noise ratio, prominence ratio) and for environmental noise (tonal audibility and tone adjustments).

families.name: Impulsiveness
families.summary: How prominent impulsive sounds are, and the adjustment applied to them in environmental noise assessment.

families.name: Psychoacoustic annoyance
families.summary: Single-number models that combine loudness, sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength and, in later models, tonality into a predicted annoyance.

families.name: Related quantities
families.summary: Quantities that psychoacoustic tools often include and that are closely tied to the metrics above.

methods.name: Zwicker loudness
methods.title: Zwicker loudness (ISO 532-1, DIN 45631)
methods.summary: Loudness from Zwicker's model: third-octave band levels are turned into specific loudness on the critical-band (Bark) scale and integrated. ISO 532-1:2017 specifies one procedure for stationary sounds and one for time-varying sounds (from which percentile values such as N5 are taken), and replaced method B of ISO 532:1975. The German standards DIN 45631 (stationary) and DIN 45631/A1 (time-varying) specify Zwicker's method; ISO 532-1:2017 states that its stationary method is based on DIN 45631:1991.
methods.notes: In China, GB/T 25982-2024 (interior noise of buses, in force since July 2025) sets loudness and sharpness limits and gives Zwicker's calculation in an informative annex.
conventions: **Sound field.** ISO 532-1 has a free-field and a diffuse-field version, which give different values for the same signal. Most implementations use free field unless told otherwise.

**Calibration.** The input is sound pressure in pascals. Audio read from a file has to be scaled first, and tools ask for this in different ways: a calibration factor, a reference level or a full-scale level.
**Sample rate.** The time-varying method is specified at 48 kHz. Some implementations reject other rates, others resample them, and the resampler changes the result slightly.

**Percentiles.** N5, the loudness exceeded 5 % of the time, depends on how the percentile is taken: SQAT picks the nearest rank, while MATLAB's `prctile` and the NumPy and Julia quantile functions interpolate, each in its own way.

**Start of the signal.** Time-varying loudness starts from silence and needs time to settle. Whether the start is left out of N5 and other statistics (`time_skip` in SQAT, `time_skip_s` in MetaSona) matters for short signals.

methods.name: Sottek Hearing Model loudness
methods.title: Loudness from the Sottek Hearing Model (ECMA-418-2)
methods.summary: Loudness from the Sottek Hearing Model defined in ECMA-418-2. The hearing model (Clause 5) produces specific loudness; the 2nd edition (2022) added a loudness calculation for sounds with tonal and noise components (Clause 8). ECMA-418-2 has had four editions in five years, so implementations of different editions can disagree.
conventions: **Edition.** The four editions give different results; compare implementations of the same edition (see the table of editions).

**Which loudness.** Clause 5 gives the hearing model's basic loudness; from the 2nd edition on, Clause 8 defines the loudness to report. MoSQITo and Mosqito.NET compute only the Clause 5 value, while the RefMap code and its ports (SQAT, sottek-hearing-model, MetaSona) compute the Clause 8 loudness.
**Start of the signal.** The filters need time to settle, so overall values leave out the first 304 ms (Section 8.1.4 of the 2025 edition, as cited by SQAT, which enforces it).
**Sample rate.** The model is defined at 48 kHz; other rates are resampled, and resamplers differ slightly.
**Sound field and channels.** The outer- and middle-ear filter can be free frontal or, from the 3rd edition, diffuse, and two channels can be combined into one binaural value. Check both settings.

methods.name: Sharpness
methods.title: Sharpness (DIN 45692, Aures, von Bismarck)
methods.summary: Sharpness is the weighted first moment of specific loudness along the critical-band rate, with a weighting that emphasises high frequencies. DIN 45692:2009 standardises the weighting and a test procedure, using Zwicker specific loudness (ISO 532-1 / DIN 45631). Most implementations also offer the weightings of von Bismarck (1974) and Aures (1985).
conventions: **Weighting.** The DIN 45692, Aures and von Bismarck weightings give different values for the same sound, and Aures' weighting depends on loudness. Many tools offer several; check which one is used (RefMap's default is Aures).

**Loudness input.** Sharpness is computed from Zwicker specific loudness, so the loudness choices (sound field, calibration, sample rate) carry over. Sharpness from another loudness model, such as ECMA-418-2 (RefMap) or Moore–Glasberg (Swift & Gee), is a different quantity.

methods.summary: Fluctuation strength describes slow modulation around 4 Hz. projects.summary: MATLAB toolbox for sound quality analysis that bundles most psychoacoustic metrics in one place: ISO 532-1 and ECMA-418-2 loudness, DIN 45692 sharpness, Daniel & Weber and ECMA-418-2 roughness, Osses fluctuation strength, Aures and ECMA-418-2 tonality, three psychoacoustic annoyance models (Zwicker & Fastl, which `main` also provides under its original attribution to Widmann; More; Di et al.) and EPNL. Every metric except the annoyance models has its own verification routine.

paper.citation: Felix Greco, G., Merino-Martínez, R., Osses, A., & Langer, S. C. (2023). SQAT: a MATLAB-based toolbox for quantitative sound quality analysis. *Proceedings of INTER-NOISE 2023*, Chiba, Japan.

notes: The README lists 61 studies and theses that use SQAT.

The latest release is v1.3 (2025-04-04); about 200 commits have been made on `main` since. Most of the metric-correctness work of August–September 2026 came from an external contributor through about 20 pull requests.
The ECMA-418-2 functions come from the RefMap MATLAB code by Lotinga and Torjussen (University of Salford); the ISO 532-1 loudness was adapted in 2023 from Ella Manor's 2015 MATLAB code for AARAE.
Open pull requests: [#78](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/78) (ECMA-418-2 fluctuation strength) and [#84](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/84) (graphical interface).
conventions: Percentile values (N5 and the others) take the nearest rank of the sorted time series, without interpolation (`get_exceeded_value`).
Statistics leave out the first `time_skip` seconds of the signal; for the ECMA-418-2 metrics at least 304 ms, which the code enforces.
caveats: The latest release (v1.3) is licensed for non-commercial use only; the GPL licence applies to the unreleased `main` branch.

`main` contains breaking fixes that are not in any release: six deviations in ISO 532-1 time-varying loudness ([#48](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/48); test signal 10 deviated by 18.14 % in v1.3), eight defects in Aures tonality ([#67](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/issues/67)), a rewrite of Daniel & Weber roughness ([#65](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/65)), the sound level meter time weighting ([#51](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/51)) and a faster annoyance calculation ([#42](https://github.com/ggrecow/SQAT/pull/42)). Results from v1.3 and `main` differ.
The README warns that `main` may contain changes that are not yet fully verified and recommends using a release.

notes: Also includes the dynamic loudness model of Chen & Hu (2012) (`DynamicLoudnessCH2012`) and partial-loudness stages after Moore, Glasberg & Baer (1997) and Chen et al. (2011) (`SpecificPartialLoudnessMGB1997`, `SpecificPartialLoudnessCHGM2011`); neither has an entry in this list.
The interface is modelled on AIM-C. Building needs libsndfile, FFTW and zlib; the Python bindings need SWIG 3.
The last commit touching the source code, bindings or Python package was on 2017-06-01; the last commit (2019-08-08) updated the README.
`swig/setup.py` names the Python package `loudness` 0.0.1, but it was never published on PyPI.
caveats: The README says "This project is still in heavy development so is not stable".
The PyPI package named `loudness` is an unrelated LUFS (ITU-R BS.1770) project (iver56/loudness); this library has to be built from source.

implements.scope: with the binaural inhibition of Moore & Glasberg (2007) for two ears
validation_details: Unit tests cover each module and model.
A validation script writes computed and expected loudness of pure tones to CSV; the expected values are labelled "Table 7" and "Example 2" without naming their source.

implements.note: Per the header, excitation patterns follow ANSI S3.4-2007, and parameter sets use the modified long-term time constants of Moore et al. (2003) and the ANSI S3.4-2007 equation for specific loudness at high levels.

derived_from: BASIC program of DIN 45631 (Zwicker et al., 1991)
validation_details: Tested against "a quick and dirty Python port of the Matlab code private by GENESIS ACOUSTICS".
implements.note: Uses 28 third-octave filters with third-order Butterworth responses after ANSI S1.11:1986; there is no time-varying (DIN 45631/A1) model.

projects.name: MoSQITo-FDP
projects.summary: Archived Python snapshot of a MoSQITo fork made for a final-degree project. It adds the Sottek Hearing Model with specific and total loudness (ECMA-418-2, 1st edition) as a step towards hearing-model tonality, and contains tone-to-noise ratio and prominence ratio after ECMA-74 Annex D.
notes: Commits run from 2021-06-13 to 2021-07-05. The package inside is still named `mosqito`, and later work went into MoSQITo itself.
The hearing-model code cites both ECMA-418-2 (1st edition, 2020) and ECMA-74 Annex F (17th edition, 2019).
Also contains the Zwicker loudness, DIN 45692 sharpness and Daniel & Weber roughness of the MoSQITo version it was forked from.
caveats: Archived snapshot without releases or maintenance.
The README marks hearing-model tonality (ECMA-74:2019 Annex G) as under development; the repository contains the hearing-model stages, but no separate tonality function was found.

implements.scope: hearing model with specific and total loudness
validation_details: Validation scripts compare the ear filter and model output with figures and values from ECMA-418-2 and ECMA-74 Annex F.
implements.note: Module `mosqito.functions.hearing_model`.

validation_details: The README lists TNR/PR as available but not validated; the tests use synthetic tones in white noise.

projects.name: PsychoacousticParametersMeasurer
projects.summary: Python scripts, commented in Spanish, that translate psychoacoustic parameters described in Zwicker and Fastl's book: Zwicker loudness (stationary and time-varying, from third-octave levels), sharpness, roughness, fluctuation strength and psychoacoustic annoyance.
notes: There is no README. The GitHub description calls the project "the translation to python of the most important parameters in the field of Psychoacoustics based on the book of Zwicker and Fastl".
Roughness (`acousticRoughness`) follows the formula in Zwicker & Fastl's book, which is not one of the roughness methods in this list.
Also contains A-weighting, voice-activity detection and the scripts Main.py and Main_WAV.py for microphone or WAV input.
caveats: No licence file, so reuse is not permitted by default.
No documentation and no stated validation.

implements.scope: stationary and time-varying, from third-octave levels
implements.note: The file header says "Loudness ISO 532-1:2014" and the filter coefficients are labelled "ISO 532-1:2014"; the published edition is ISO 532-1:2017.
The file header says "Sharpness DIN 45692"; the function also returns the von Bismarck and Aures variants.
The header cites Zwicker & Fastl, "Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models", without naming an edition.
The header cites Zwicker & Fastl, "Psychoacoustics: Facts and Models", without naming an edition.

projects.name: PsySound3
projects.license_note: The repository has no licence file, only a no-warranty disclaimer (`README-NO_WARRANTY`). The licence of the original Google Code project was not checked.
projects.summary: MATLAB program with a graphical interface for analysing sound recordings. Its analysers include the Chalupper–Fastl dynamic loudness model, Moore–Glasberg–Baer loudness and Daniel & Weber roughness.

paper.citation: PsySound3: a program for the analysis of sound recordings (2008). Acoustics'08 abstract, *The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America*, 123(5_Supplement), 3247.

notes: The GitHub repository is an automatic export of the Google Code project `psysound3`; its commits run from January 2009 to March 2015. It also bundles MIRtoolbox functions.
`@LoudnessMG` computes loudness with a "Moore et al. static model" adapted from PsySound2; the model version is not stated.

Search results describe PsySound3 as also covering sharpness and fluctuation strength. In this mirror, the descriptions of `@LoudnessCF` and `@LoudnessMG` list sharpness among their outputs; a fluctuation-strength analyser was not confirmed.
caveats: `README-BUGSISSUES` lists open problems, including "Various Accuracy Bugs", "Calibration Problems" and "Revisit calibration modes".
The project states no validation, and there have been no commits since March 2015.
With no licence file, the terms for reuse and redistribution are unclear.

implements.note: The analyser names J. Chalupper and H. Fastl as authors.

Also cites Glasberg & Moore (1990) for the auditory filters. The analyser description says it covers time-varying and binaural loudness, and it also cites Glasberg & Moore (2002) and Moore & Glasberg (2007).
The same analyser as the stationary entry; its description cites Glasberg & Moore (2002).
Adapted for PsySound3 by Matt Flax (2006), with changes by Farhan Rizwi (2007). AARAE's `RoughnessDW.m` is a port of this analyser.

projects.name: python-acoustics
projects.summary: General Python library for acousticians, published on PyPI as `acoustics`. For this list it is relevant for its tonal audibility and tonal adjustment after ISO 1996-2:2007. Archived in February 2024 and continued as acoustic-toolbox.
notes: The successor is [acoustic-toolbox](https://github.com/Universite-Gustave-Eiffel/acoustic-toolbox), which continues the same code.
It has no loudness, sharpness or roughness modules.
caveats: The repository was archived on 2024-02-07 and is read-only.
A fix to the default window of the tonality code (2023-08-20) is on the default branch but not in the last PyPI release (0.2.6, July 2022).
It follows ISO 1996-2:2007, which has been withdrawn; ISO 1996-2:2017 replaced its tonal audibility method with those of Annexes J and K.

validation_details: A test of the examples in the standard, using DELTA tone files, is commented out.
implements.note: Module `acoustics.standards.iso_1996_2_2007`. The `Tonality` docstring uses the title of Annex C ("Objective method for assessing the audibility of tones in noise"), though the code does not name the annex.

projects.name: Specific loudness of time-varying sounds (MATLAB tool)
projects.license_note: Licence of the HAW Hamburg repository record; the archive itself has no licence file.
projects.summary: MATLAB tool with a graphical interface, from HAW Hamburg, that shows the specific loudness of time-varying sounds: a Moore–Glasberg front end on ERB bands with temporal processing after Glasberg & Moore (2002), Chalupper & Fastl (2002) or Baumgarte (2000). Written in 2007 for a diploma thesis and published on Zenodo in 2022.

paper.citation: Sabrautzky, C. (2007). *Erweiterung eines Lautheitsmodells von Moore und Glasberg zur Berechnung der spezifischen Lautheit dynamischer Audiosignale* [Diploma thesis, HAW Hamburg].

notes: Code by Christian Sabrautzky (2007, revision 0.7), with changes by Robert Mores (2013) and a playback toolbar by Nico Schäfer. The Zenodo record (2022-12-16) includes an English overview of the models and the German thesis.
Offers free-field and diffuse-field outer-ear filters and three spectral analyses: FFT with a Blackman–Harris or Hann window, and a Fourier-time transform.
caveats: Not an implementation of ANSI S3.4-2007 or ISO 532-2/-3. It follows Glasberg & Moore (2002) with the constants A, α and E_THRQ read from published graphs and interpolated, and its Chalupper–Fastl and Baumgarte options apply those models' temporal processing to Moore–Glasberg specific loudness.
conventions: Input must be sampled at 32 kHz; the reference level is entered as the sound pressure level of a full-scale sine.

implements.scope: specific loudness over time on ERB bands; three temporal models
validation_details: The thesis compares the total loudness of pure tones (30–100 dB) with LOUDAES, Glasberg & Moore's program for stationary sounds: mostly within 5 %, with larger deviations at low levels near 50 Hz and above 5 kHz (−9.3 % for 5 kHz at 30 dB).
For two equal-level tones at 1 and 2 kHz, the deviation from LOUDAES ranges from −4.4 % to +3.8 % with the Hann-window FFT and reaches +6.7 % with the Fourier-time transform.
For the stationary part of signals the thesis reports good agreement with TVL, Glasberg & Moore's program for time-varying sounds, without figures.

projects.name: SUAVE
projects.summary: Python environment for the multi-fidelity conceptual design of aircraft ("An Aerospace Vehicle Environment"). Its noise tools compute perceived noise level (PNL), tone-corrected PNL (PNLT) and effective perceived noise level (EPNL) from one-third-octave spectra.
notes: The noise tools are in `SUAVE/Methods/Noise/Fidelity_One/Noise_Tools`, written by C. Ilario (2015) and modified by E. Botero (2016). The same folder has SENEL, dBA and noise-certification-limit helpers.
caveats: Development appears to have stopped in 2022: the last release (2.5.2) is from March 2022 and the last commit from December 2022.
No validation of the noise metrics is stated.

implements.note: EPNL is computed from a PNLT time history. The noise tools cite neither ICAO Annex 16 nor 14 CFR Part 36, nor an edition; their docstrings give "Source: None".

projects.name: Zwicker's Loudness Calculation SW + Tool (ISO 532B)
projects.language_note: C console program for BSD, Linux and Windows that reads one-third-octave band levels from files.
projects.license_note: SourceForge lists "GNU General Public License version 2.0"; whether later versions are allowed was not checked.
projects.summary: Console program in C, for BSD, Linux and Windows, that calculates the loudness of stationary sounds with Zwicker's method (ISO 532B / DIN 45631) from one-third-octave band levels. A companion tool analyses WAV files to produce those input files.
notes: Partly ported from the BASIC "Program for calculating loudness according to DIN 45631 (ISO 532B)", published in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of Japan in 1991, as obtained from Osaka University's website.

Distributed as release archives on SourceForge, from release 010 (2010-04-15) to zwickerloudness-020 (2011-07-01). The last-commit date given here (2018-06-05) is the project's "Last Update" date on SourceForge, not a commit date.
caveats: Stationary sounds only; there is no procedure for time-varying sounds.
No validation is stated on the SourceForge pages; the README inside the release archive was not reviewed for this entry.

derived_from: BASIC program of DIN 45631 (Zwicker et al., 1991)
implements.note: Port of the 1991 BASIC program "according to DIN 45631 (ISO 532B)", the program that accompanies DIN 45631:1991; the same program is the basis of deeuu/loudness.

projects.name: PsychoBox
projects.summary: Desktop application (PySide6 GUI) for playing, editing, filtering and analysing audio. Its psychoacoustic metrics are computed by MoSQITo 1.2.1: Zwicker loudness, ECMA-418-2 loudness, DIN 45692 sharpness, Daniel & Weber roughness and ECMA-418-2 roughness.
notes: `requirements.txt` pins `mosqito==1.2.1`; PsychoBox itself states no standard editions.
Also does recording and binaural playback correction. An install guide and a tutorial (PDF) are in the Documentation folder.
Listed as an end-user application, although its metric values come from MoSQITo. Wrappers that are neither an application nor an established library are recorded in `data/ignored.yaml` instead.
caveats: All metric values come from MoSQITo 1.2.1, whose ECMA-418-2 functions follow the 2nd edition (2022), two editions behind the current one.

implements.note: Calls `loudness_zwst` of MoSQITo 1.2.1.
Calls `loudness_ecma` of MoSQITo 1.2.1 (ECMA-418-2:2022, Clause 5 only).
Calls `sharpness_din_st` of MoSQITo 1.2.1 with the DIN weighting.
Calls `roughness_dw` of MoSQITo 1.2.1.
Calls `roughness_ecma` of MoSQITo 1.2.1, whose bibliography cites ECMA-418-2:2022.

projects.name: Soundscapy
projects.summary: Python library for soundscape assessment. Its optional audio module computes psychoacoustic metrics of binaural recordings, per channel, by calling MoSQITo: time-varying Zwicker loudness, DIN 45692 sharpness and Daniel & Weber roughness.
projects.ai_note: Commit metadata only; the README does not mention AI. At least 31 commits from March to May 2026 carry co-author lines for Claude or Copilot, and eight commits are authored by copilot-swe-agent[bot].

paper.citation: Mitchell, A., Aletta, F., & Kang, J. (2022). How to analyse and represent quantitative soundscape data. *JASA Express Letters*, 2, 037201.

notes: The psychoacoustic functions need the optional `audio` extra (MoSQITo 1.2.1 or newer). Environmental acoustic metrics come from acoustic-toolbox and ecoacoustic indices from scikit-maad.
Issue [#123](https://github.com/MitchellAcoustics/Soundscapy/issues/123), open since 2025-10-29, plans to integrate sottek-hearing-model for ECMA-418-2 metrics; its branch has no such code yet.
The paper the README asks users to cite covers soundscape data analysis, not the psychoacoustic functions.
caveats: The psychoacoustic values are computed by MoSQITo, so their editions and accuracy are those of the installed MoSQITo version.

implements.note: Calls `loudness_zwtv`.
Calls `sharpness_din_from_loudness`, `sharpness_din_perseg` or `sharpness_din_tv`; the weighting can be chosen.
Calls `roughness_dw`.

projects.name: ZwickerLoudnessAudio.jl
projects.license_note: The README credits MoSQITo (Apache-2.0) for the transcribed time-varying filter tables.
projects.summary: Julia front end to ZwickerLoudness.jl that computes ISO 532-1:2017 Zwicker loudness from waveforms or WAV files: stationary loudness, and since v0.3.0 time-varying loudness with N5 and N10.
notes: Depends on ZwickerLoudness.jl (compat 0.3), which does the loudness calculation from band levels; this package computes the band levels.
First registered in the Julia General registry as version 0.2.0 (2026-06-01).

implements.scope: stationary, from a waveform or WAV file
validation_details: ISO 532-1 Annex B signals 2–5, synthesised in-process, are within the standard's ±5 % (+2.9 %, +3.6 %, +0.5 % and +2.6 % per the README).
conventions: Stationary loudness resamples input below 48 kHz to 48 kHz (polyphase), with a warning.
implements.note: Computes the third-octave levels itself (per-band Butterworth filters of order 3 by default, as in MoSQITo) and passes them to ZwickerLoudness.jl for the loudness.

implements.scope: time-varying, from a waveform or WAV file at 48 kHz
validation_details: Cross-checked end to end with MoSQITo `loudness_zwtv` (N(t) about 3e-16 relative, N5/N10 about 2e-15 absolute).
An Annex B.4 test is skipped when the ISO recording is not available locally.
conventions: Time-varying loudness accepts 48 kHz input only (an error otherwise).
implements.note: The Annex A filter cascade is transcribed from MoSQITo (`_third_octave_levels`, `_square_and_smooth`).

cite.text: The README links a [Zenodo DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/latestdoi/1253784080) for the latest version.

projects.name: PsyTools
projects.access_note: It redirects to the TU Graz GitLab login page, while the author's profile page on the same server is public (checked 2026-10-07).
projects.claim: A conference paper describes an open-source Python toolbox for standardised psychoacoustic analysis: loudness, sharpness, fluctuation strength, roughness, tonality, psychoacoustic annoyance, LAeq and LAmax, following ISO 532-1, DIN 45692 and ECMA-418, with the Zwicker model and the Sottek Hearing Model.
projects.standing_note: Described in a conference paper in May 2026.
projects.summary: Python toolbox for psychoacoustic analysis from TU Graz, described in a 2026 student conference paper.

paper.citation: Stangl, E.-M., & Donnerer, J. (2026). PsyTools: An open-source Python toolbox for standardized psychoacoustic analysis. *POSTERS 2026: Proceedings of the International Student Scientific Conference Poster*, Czech Technical University in Prague, 172–173.

leads.name: Genesis Loudness Toolbox
leads.claim: Free MATLAB toolbox (2010) said to cover ISO 532B / DIN 45631, ANSI S3.4-2007, Zwicker's time-varying model, Glasberg & Moore (2002) and Boullet's (2006) loudness model for impulsive sounds.
leads.why: An [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20150306205824/http://genesis-acoustics.com/index.php?page=32) of the page (2015) says the ZIP file contains MATLAB source files, validation WAV files and a Readme with the terms of use, but the download page was not archived and the website could not be reached, so the code and its licence could not be checked.

leads.claim: Functions named `loudness_1991` (Zwicker loudness, free or diffuse field), `sharpness_Fastl` and `roughness4`.
leads.why: The page describes the functions, but its "Download the MATLAB codes" item has no link, also in an [archived copy](https://web.archive.org/web/20250709072252/https://acoustics.salford.ac.uk/psychoacoustics/sound-quality-making-products-sound-better/an-introduction-to-sound-quality-testing/matlab-codes/) of July 2025, so the code could not be obtained.

updates.title: Version 0.3: who ported code from whom, how to cite it, and five more projects
updates.body:
Method pages now show who ported code from whom, as the projects state it. A comparison with related code is
marked "(its source)", "(a port of it)" or "(also ported from …)", and its tag is grey when nothing independent
is stated: agreement with the code an implementation was ported from shows a faithful port, not that either
follows the standard. A new section, *Before you compare numbers*, lists the choices that make correct
implementations give different numbers: sound field, calibration, sample rate, percentile definition,
sharpness weighting and the start of the signal.

Also in this version:

- Every project page has a *How to cite* line, and all standards, model papers and software papers are
  available as BibTeX in references.bib.
- New projects: the ITA-Toolbox (RWTH Aachen, MATLAB), Mosqito.NET (a C# port of MoSQITo, newly released), and
  two legacy MATLAB tools, the Swift & Gee loudness and sharpness codes and the HAW Hamburg loudness tool.
  PsyTools (TU Graz) is listed in a new group, *Status unknown*, because its repository cannot be opened
  without a login.
- SQAT and MoSQITo, which are widely used, and sottek-hearing-model, a very good implementation, are shown in
  bold and first in every list. In personal use, the maintainer of the list found sottek-hearing-model in very
  good agreement with HEAD acoustics ArtemiS SUITE. The Auditory Modeling Toolbox and the ITA-Toolbox, widely
  used toolboxes that also include some psychoacoustic functions, are listed with the other established
  projects.
- Each project page explains its kind: library/toolbox, research code, application, plug-in or reference
  program. MATLAB toolboxes and Python packages share the kind library/toolbox, since both are used the same
  way.
- Newly released projects are described as not yet seen to be widely used.
- The FAQ answer on which code to use starts from the reader's language and use, and names projects built for
  a particular use.
- Validation details were added for MoSQITo's ECMA-418-2 roughness and for phonometry's tone-to-noise and
  prominence ratios, psychoacoustic annoyance and ISO 226:2023 contours. phonometry's annoyance is now listed
  under its own tests only, as no published value is checked.
- RefMap's Python functions use the sottek-hearing-model package and are listed under it.
- The twice-monthly refresh now checks every external link and reports broken ones in its review issue.

updates.title: Version 0.2: how each implementation was validated
updates.body:
Project and method pages have a new section, *How it was validated*: what each project says it checked, and
against what (test signals of the standard, the model authors' code, MoSQITo, SQAT or commercial software),
with the tolerances and results it reports. Validation tags now name what an implementation was compared with,
for example "compared with MoSQITo", instead of "another implementation". Agreement with another implementation
shows that both compute the same values, not that either follows the standard.

Also in this version:

- On the home page, "+ more" shows the remaining projects of an edition in place.
- Edition labels in the implementation tables link to the standard or paper. Zwicker & Fastl (1999) now has its
  DOI, and five model papers and theses link to their publisher or library pages; the rest link to their full
  reference on the Standards page.
- MetaSona is listed as a C library with a Python interface.
- PsychoacousticMetrics.jl and Kirin Hypha, two newly released projects, were added the same day.

updates.title: Two newly released projects
updates.body:
PsychoacousticMetrics.jl (Julia) adds DIN 45692 sharpness, Daniel & Weber roughness, Osses et al. (2016)
fluctuation strength and Widmann (1992) psychoacoustic annoyance on top of ZwickerLoudness.jl, by the same
author. Kirin Hypha, a measurement plug-in for audio workstations, computes ISO 532-1 time-varying loudness and
DIN 45692 sharpness in Rust, ported from MoSQITo. Both were found by the first scheduled search for new
projects; like the other newly released projects, they are not yet seen to be widely used.

updates.title: Version 0.1, the first public version of LISQM
updates.body:
LISQM (List of Implementations of Sound Quality Metrics) starts with 32 projects in Python, MATLAB, Octave, C,
C++, Rust, Julia and Pure Data, and 22 methods from Zwicker loudness to aural detectability. Every implementation is
tied to the standard edition or model paper it follows, with links to the documentation the facts were taken
from. Repository dates, releases and package versions are refreshed twice a month.

Worth knowing as of today:

- ECMA-418-2 is at its 4th edition (June 2025), which added fluctuation strength. sottek-hearing-model and
  refmap-psychoacoustics follow it, as do phonometry and MetaSona, two newly released projects that are not yet
  seen to be widely used. SQAT has it on its main branch only, and MoSQITo still follows the 2nd edition (2022).
- SQAT's latest release (v1.3) is licensed for non-commercial use only. Its main branch is GPL-3.0 and
  carries unreleased fixes to ISO 532-1 time-varying loudness, Aures tonality and Daniel & Weber roughness
  that change results.
- All three parts of ISO 532 are being revised; committee drafts have existed since November 2024.
- No open implementation was found for DIN 38455:2024 (the first German roughness standard), DIN 45681 or
  ISO/TS 20065:2022.
- Six projects disclose that AI tools assisted their development; each project page says where.
- Every project is in one group: established, newly released (first released less than about a year ago and
  not yet seen to be widely used), developing, legacy (archived, or no commit for three years) or others
  (calls another listed project). Lists follow this order, so a new, little-used or unmaintained project is
  never the first suggestion.
- Candidates that could not be checked yet, such as PsyTools (TU Graz) and the ITA-Toolbox, are listed on
  the About page as leads.
